questions.question: What are design patterns and why do they matter?
questions.title: What are design patterns in software development?
questions.direct_answer: Design patterns are reusable solutions to common software design problems. They are not code you copy — they are templates for structuring classes and objects. They matter because they give developers a shared vocabulary and proven solutions, making code easier to communicate, understand, and maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand patterns as concepts, not copy-paste code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking patterns are code libraries you import
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Gang of Four (GoF) book as the origin of the 23 classic patterns

sections.title: What Design Patterns Really Are
sections.content:
Design patterns are **proven templates** for solving recurring design problems in software. Think of them like architectural blueprints: an architect doesn't reinvent how to build a staircase every time — they use a proven design adapted to the building. Similarly, design patterns give you battle-tested structures for common code challenges. They're **not libraries** you import or code you copy-paste; they're conceptual solutions you implement in your own way. The **Gang of Four (GoF)** — four authors who wrote the foundational 1994 book — catalogued 23 classic patterns that are still relevant today.

In Java Spring Boot development, you'll see these patterns everywhere: **Singleton** for beans, **Factory** for object creation, **Proxy** for transactions. Learning patterns means you speak the same language as senior developers, making code reviews faster and design discussions clearer.

emerald|Value|~Shared vocabulary|faster reviews|easier onboarding|recognise solutions
violet|In Spring|~Patterns everywhere|Singleton beans|Factory context|Proxy @Transactional

sections.title: Simple Factory Pattern Example
When Design Patterns Matter
sections.content: Use design patterns when you're solving a problem that's been solved many times before — don't reinvent the wheel. In a **Spring Boot e-commerce app**, you'd use **Strategy** pattern for different discount calculation rules (percentage off, fixed amount, buy-one-get-one), **Observer** for sending order confirmation emails when an order is placed, and **Builder** for constructing complex configuration objects. Patterns shine when code needs to be **extended without modification** (Open-Closed Principle) or when multiple developers need to **understand the structure quickly** without lengthy explanations. If you're writing a one-time script, patterns might be overkill; but in production codebases with multiple contributors, they're essential for maintainability.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating patterns as copy-paste code**: Freshers often search for "Singleton code in Java" and copy it without understanding why or when to use it — patterns are concepts you adapt, not snippets you paste.
- **Overusing patterns**: Applying patterns where simple code would work is called the Golden Hammer anti-pattern — not every problem needs a Factory or Strategy.
- **Not connecting patterns to Spring**: In interviews, freshers discuss patterns abstractly but can't name which patterns Spring Boot uses internally (Singleton for beans, Proxy for transactions), missing the practical connection that interviewers want to see.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Template not library**: Design patterns are conceptual solutions you implement yourself, not pre-built code you import from a package
- **Gang of Four (GoF)**: The 1994 book that catalogued 23 foundational patterns still used today in Java development
- **Shared vocabulary**: Saying 'use a Factory here' is faster than explaining 'create an object that creates other objects based on input'
- **Spring uses patterns**: Spring Boot internally implements Singleton, Factory, Proxy, Template Method — knowing patterns helps you understand the framework
- **Not one-size-fits-all**: Patterns solve specific problems; using the wrong pattern or overusing patterns creates complexity instead of clarity
- **Maintenance benefit**: Patterns make code predictable — a developer familiar with Strategy pattern can understand your discount logic in minutes
- **Interview currency**: Interviewers expect you to know common patterns and where they appear in Spring Boot applications

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Design patterns are reusable templates for solving common design problems in software. They're not libraries or code you copy — they're proven structures you adapt to your needs. The Gang of Four book from 1994 catalogued 23 classic patterns that we still use today. Think of patterns like architectural blueprints: an architect doesn't reinvent how to build a staircase every time, they use a proven design. In Java development, you'll see patterns everywhere. Spring Boot uses Singleton for all beans by default, Factory pattern in the ApplicationContext to create those beans, and Proxy pattern when you use the at-Transactional annotation for database transactions. Patterns matter because they give teams a shared vocabulary. Instead of explaining 'we need a class that creates different payment processors based on user selection,' you just say 'let's use a Factory pattern' and everyone immediately understands. They also make code easier to maintain because other developers recognise the structure. The mistake freshers make is thinking patterns are just code snippets to memorise. They're actually conceptual tools that you implement differently each time based on context. In an interview, connect patterns to real Spring Boot examples to show you understand how they're used in production, not just in textbooks.

speakable_v2.hook: Design patterns aren't code you copy — they're proven templates that let two developers understand each other's structure instantly.

beats.content: The Gang of Four book from 1994 documented 23 classic patterns. The authors catalogued solutions that kept showing up across different codebases and gave each one a name. That naming is the real power.

If you and a teammate both know the Singleton pattern, one of you can say 'I used Singleton here' and the other instantly understands the structure without reading a line of code. That shared vocabulary speeds up design discussions, code reviews, and onboarding.

content: Creational patterns — control how objects are created (Singleton, Factory, Builder)
Structural patterns — control how objects are composed (Decorator, Adapter, Facade)
Behavioral patterns — control how objects interact (Strategy, Observer, Template Method)

questions.question: What are the three categories of GoF design patterns?
questions.title: Creational, Structural, and Behavioral design patterns
questions.direct_answer: GoF patterns are in three categories: Creational (how objects are created — Singleton, Factory, Builder), Structural (how objects are assembled — Adapter, Decorator, Facade), and Behavioral (how objects interact — Strategy, Observer, Template Method). Each category solves a different dimension of design.

interviewer_intent.testing: Recall of the three categories and at least 2 patterns per category
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up which pattern belongs to which category
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a one-line description of each category and 2-3 examples per category without prompting

sections.title: The Three Pattern Categories
sections.content:
The Gang of Four organised their 23 patterns into three categories based on what problem each solves. **Creational patterns** control how objects are created — they give you flexibility in object instantiation (Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype, Abstract Factory). **Structural patterns** focus on how classes and objects are composed — they help you build larger structures from smaller pieces (Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge, Flyweight). **Behavioral patterns** define how objects communicate and distribute responsibility — they're about interaction and algorithms (Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method, Iterator, State, Chain of Responsibility, Mediator, Memento, Visitor, Interpreter). Each category addresses a different dimension: creation vs. composition vs. interaction.

In a Spring Boot cart service, you might use **Factory** (creational) to create different payment processors, **Decorator** (structural) to add logging around service calls, and **Observer** (behavioral) to notify users when their cart is about to expire.

sections.title: Three GoF Categories at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Creational|~How objects are made|Singleton, Factory|Builder, Prototype|5 GoF patterns
blue|Structural|~How objects compose|Adapter, Decorator|Facade, Proxy|7 GoF patterns
emerald|Behavioral|~How objects interact|Strategy, Observer|Command, Template|11 GoF patterns
violet|Tip|~State the category|creation?|composition?|communication?

sections.title: One Pattern from Each Category
When to Use Each Category
sections.content:
Use **Creational patterns** when object creation is complex or needs to be controlled — for example, use **Builder** when constructing an Order with many optional fields (gift wrap, express shipping, custom message), or **Factory** when the exact class to instantiate depends on runtime conditions (payment method chosen by user).

Use **Structural patterns** when you need to compose objects or adapt interfaces — **Adapter** when integrating a third-party payment gateway with a different interface than your code expects, or **Facade** to simplify a complex subsystem like order processing (payment, inventory, shipping) behind a single OrderService interface.

Use **Behavioral patterns** when you need flexible algorithms or communication — **Strategy** for interchangeable discount rules, **Observer** to notify multiple systems (email, SMS, analytics) when an order is placed.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Misclassifying patterns**: Freshers often think Observer is structural because it 'connects' objects, but it's behavioral because it defines how objects communicate at runtime.
- **Confusing similar patterns**: Mixing up Adapter (converts one interface to another) with Decorator (adds responsibilities to an object) because both wrap objects.
- **Only memorising names**: Listing pattern names without understanding which category or what problem each solves — interviewers will ask 'why would you use Factory instead of Builder' to test real understanding, not just recall.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Creational patterns**: Control object creation — Singleton, Factory, Builder, Prototype, Abstract Factory solve instantiation problems
- **Structural patterns**: Compose objects into larger structures — Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge, Flyweight solve composition problems
- **Behavioral patterns**: Define object communication — Strategy, Observer, Command, Template Method, Iterator, State solve interaction problems
- **23 total GoF patterns**: 5 creational, 7 structural, 11 behavioral patterns in the original Gang of Four catalogue
- **Categories not exclusive**: Some patterns have traits of multiple categories, but GoF assigned each to one primary category based on main intent
- **Spring uses all three**: Singleton and Factory (creational), Proxy (structural), Template Method and Observer (behavioral) are all in Spring Boot
- **Interview tip**: When asked about a pattern, immediately state its category to show you understand the taxonomy

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Gang of Four organised their 23 patterns into three categories based on what problem each solves. Creational patterns deal with how objects are created. They give you control over instantiation — examples are Singleton, Factory, and Builder. In Spring Boot, every bean is a Singleton by default, and the ApplicationContext acts as a Factory creating those beans. Structural patterns focus on how you compose classes and objects into larger structures. Think Adapter, Decorator, Facade, and Proxy. Spring uses Proxy heavily — when you put at-Transactional on a method, Spring wraps your class in a proxy that handles the transaction boundaries. Behavioral patterns are about how objects communicate and divide responsibility. Examples include Strategy, Observer, Template Method, and Command. Spring Events use the Observer pattern — you publish an event and multiple listeners can react to it. The key difference: creational is about creation, structural is about composition, and behavioral is about interaction. The mistake freshers make is mixing these up, like calling Observer a structural pattern because it connects objects. It's behavioral because it defines runtime communication. In an interview, when you mention a pattern, always state its category to show you understand the bigger picture, not just isolated pattern names.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Three categories cover all 23 GoF patterns — and knowing which bucket each belongs to is the first thing interviewers check.

beats.content: For Java backend interviews, focus on Creational and Behavioral first. Singleton and Factory come up in almost every Spring conversation. Strategy and Observer are the behavioral ones interviewers reach for most.

questions.question: What is the difference between a pattern and a framework?
questions.title: Pattern vs framework
questions.direct_answer: A pattern is a reusable solution concept you implement yourself; a framework is pre-written code that calls your code, applying patterns for you as part of its structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Conceptual clarity about patterns vs tools — a common confusion for freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking Spring is a pattern or that learning Spring means you've learned the patterns it uses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out that Spring implements several GoF patterns internally — IoC container, Factory, Proxy

sections.title: You Implement Patterns, Frameworks Use Patterns
sections.content:
A **design pattern** is a conceptual solution you implement in your own code — it's like a recipe you follow to bake a cake. You write the classes, define the interfaces, and structure the relationships. The **Singleton pattern** tells you 'create one instance and provide global access,' but you write the code that does it. A **framework** is pre-written, reusable code that provides structure and calls your code — it's like a pre-made cake mix where you just add your ingredients. **Spring Boot** is a framework: it creates objects, manages their lifecycle, and calls your methods at the right time.

The key difference is **control flow**: with patterns, **you call the code** (you instantiate the Singleton when you need it); with frameworks, **the framework calls your code** (Spring instantiates your beans and injects them). Frameworks **use patterns internally** — Spring uses Singleton for bean scope, Factory to create beans, Proxy for AOP, Template Method in JdbcTemplate. Learning a framework doesn't mean you've learned the patterns; understanding patterns helps you understand how the framework works and design your own components better.

sections.title: Pattern vs Framework at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pattern|~A concept|you implement it|no jar to import|full control
blue|Framework|~Pre-written code|calls your code|configure + extend|constrained by it
emerald|Control flow|~Who calls whom|pattern: you call in|framework: it calls you|Hollywood Principle
violet|Spring|~A framework|uses Singleton/Factory|uses Proxy (AOP)|uses Observer (events)

sections.title: Pattern vs Framework in Code
Pattern vs Framework
sections.content:
| Aspect | Design Pattern | Framework |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | Conceptual solution template | Pre-written reusable code library |
| Control flow | You call the pattern code | Framework calls your code |
| Implementation | You write the code yourself | You configure and extend framework |
| Example | Singleton, Factory, Strategy | Spring Boot, Hibernate, JUnit |
| Flexibility | Full control over implementation | Constrained by framework design |

sections.title: When to Choose Each
sections.content:
Use **design patterns** when you're writing application code and need to structure your own classes — for example, implementing a **Factory** to create different report generators (PDF, Excel, CSV) in your cart service, or using **Strategy** for custom discount calculation logic. You have full control and write all the code.

Use a **framework** when you need infrastructure and don't want to reinvent the wheel — **Spring Boot** for dependency injection and web apps, **Hibernate** for database mapping, **JUnit** for testing. The framework provides the plumbing, you provide the business logic. Often you do both: use **Spring Boot framework** to manage your application structure, and use **design patterns** within your services to organise business logic. For example, Spring handles bean creation (Framework), but you implement a **Strategy pattern** for discount rules (Pattern you write).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Spring a pattern**: Saying 'Spring is a design pattern' when it's a framework that uses patterns — shows confusion about vocabulary and concepts.
- **Thinking framework knowledge equals pattern knowledge**: A fresher who's used Spring but can't explain the Singleton pattern Spring uses internally hasn't truly understood patterns.
- **Not recognising patterns in frameworks**: Using at-Transactional daily without knowing it's the Proxy pattern means you're missing opportunities to understand and apply patterns in your own code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Pattern is a concept**: You implement it yourself — it's a template or blueprint you adapt to your code
- **Framework is code**: Pre-written library that provides structure and calls your code — you extend and configure it
- **Inversion of Control**: With patterns you call the code; with frameworks the code calls you (Hollywood Principle: 'don't call us, we'll call you')
- **Frameworks use patterns**: Spring uses Singleton (bean scope), Factory (ApplicationContext), Proxy (AOP), Template Method (JdbcTemplate)
- **Learning both matters**: Understanding patterns helps you use frameworks more effectively and design better application code
- **Spring Boot is a framework**: It provides infrastructure for dependency injection, web servers, data access — not a pattern itself
- **Interview clarity**: Distinguish 'Spring uses Singleton pattern' from 'Spring is a Singleton' — precision matters in technical discussions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A design pattern is a conceptual solution that you implement yourself. It's a template you follow to structure your code. If you're implementing the Singleton pattern, you write the class with a private constructor, a static instance variable, and a public method to get that instance. You control every line of code. A framework is different. It's pre-written code that provides structure and calls your methods at the right time. Spring Boot is a framework. You don't write the dependency injection code or the web server — Spring provides that. You just annotate your classes with at-Service or at-Controller, and Spring handles instantiation and injection. The key difference is control flow. With a pattern, you call the code — you instantiate your Singleton when you need it. With a framework, the framework calls your code — Spring creates your beans and injects them without you explicitly calling new. The important thing is that frameworks use patterns internally. Spring uses Singleton for bean scope by default, Factory pattern in the ApplicationContext to create beans, and Proxy pattern when you use at-Transactional. So learning patterns helps you understand how Spring works under the hood. The mistake freshers make is thinking that using Spring means they understand the patterns Spring uses. You can use Spring for years without really understanding Singleton or Proxy if you never look deeper. In an interview, show you understand the difference. Say 'Spring Boot is a framework that uses several GoF patterns internally, like Singleton for bean management and Proxy for AOP.' That shows you know both what Spring is and what patterns it's built on.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Freshers often think Spring IS the patterns — but Spring is a framework that uses patterns internally, and that's a big difference.

beats.content: A pattern is a concept you implement yourself — there's no jar to add to your pom.xml. A framework is actual pre-written code you configure and extend. The key rule: with a library, your code calls it. With a framework, it calls your code. Spring controls the lifecycle; you just plug in your logic.

The interesting link is that Spring itself is built using patterns. Its IoC container is Factory pattern. AOP proxies are Proxy pattern. ApplicationEventPublisher is Observer. Knowing this means you understand why Spring works the way it does, not just how to use it.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: Thinking Spring Boot teaches you patterns. It applies patterns for you. To understand why Spring behaves the way it does, you need to understand the underlying patterns it's built on.

questions.question: Why should you learn design patterns as a fresher Java developer?
questions.title: Why freshers should learn design patterns
questions.direct_answer: Design patterns give you a shared vocabulary for code structure, help you recognise proven solutions to common problems, and prepare you for codebases and interview questions that use them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can articulate the value of patterns beyond just memorising them
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying patterns are important without explaining what specific value they provide
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention vocabulary and communication — patterns make code reviews and design discussions faster

sections.title: Why Patterns Matter for Your Career
sections.content:
Learning design patterns as a fresher is an investment in your career, not just interview prep. First, patterns give you a **shared vocabulary** with other developers.

Instead of explaining 'we need a class that creates different types of payment processors based on user input,' you say 'let's use a Factory pattern' and everyone immediately understands. Code reviews become faster and clearer. Second, patterns help you **recognise solutions** in existing code. When you join a company and see **@Transactional** everywhere, knowing it's the **Proxy pattern** helps you understand what's happening behind the scenes. Third, patterns are **interview currency** — interviewers expect you to know Singleton, Factory, Strategy, and Observer at minimum. Fourth, patterns prevent you from **reinventing the wheel**. The problems they solve (flexible object creation, adding behavior without modification, decoupled communication) appear constantly in production code. Finally, understanding patterns helps you **learn frameworks faster** — recognising that Spring uses Singleton, Factory, and Proxy means you understand Spring's design, not just its API.

sections.title: Why Freshers Learn Patterns
sections.content:
amber|Vocabulary|~Shared language|'use a Factory'|faster reviews|design discussions
blue|Recognise code|~Read faster|spot Proxy in @Transactional|understand intent|onboard quickly
emerald|Interview currency|~Expected basics|Singleton, Factory|Strategy, Observer|common questions
violet|Caution|~Don't over-apply|judgment > breadth|simple code often wins|learn to communicate

sections.title: Pattern Vocabulary in Code Reviews
When Pattern Knowledge Helps You
sections.content: Patterns help in **code reviews** — when a senior developer says 'this God Class should be split using Single Responsibility' or 'use a Factory here instead of new everywhere,' you understand immediately. Patterns help in **job interviews** — most Java interviews ask about Singleton, Factory, or Spring-related patterns. Patterns help **reading existing code** — when you see a class wrapping another class, you recognise the Decorator or Proxy pattern and understand the intent. Patterns help in **design discussions** — your team debates whether to use Strategy or Command pattern for handling user actions, and you can participate meaningfully. Patterns help **learning new frameworks** — when you learn React or Angular later, you'll recognise Observer pattern (state management) and already understand the concept, just learning new syntax.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Memorising without understanding**: Cramming pattern names and definitions for interviews but not understanding when or why to use them — interviewers test application, not recall.
- **Only learning for interviews**: Thinking patterns are just interview questions instead of practical tools for structuring code — then struggling when codebases use patterns you can't recognise.
- **Not practising in code**: Reading about patterns but never implementing them means you can't explain them conversationally or debug issues in pattern-based code at work.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Shared vocabulary**: Saying 'use a Factory' is clearer and faster than explaining object creation logic in meetings and code reviews
- **Recognise solutions**: Seeing patterns in existing code helps you understand codebases faster when joining a team
- **Interview necessity**: Most Java interviews include pattern questions — Singleton, Factory, Strategy, Observer are common topics
- **Framework understanding**: Knowing patterns helps you understand Spring Boot, Hibernate, and other frameworks that use patterns internally
- **Don't reinvent**: Patterns provide proven solutions to common problems, saving you from creating inferior custom solutions
- **Career progression**: Senior developers expect you to know patterns — not knowing them limits your growth and contributions
- **Practical application**: Patterns aren't just theory — you'll use them in production code for creating objects, adding behavior, and decoupling components

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: As a fresher, learning design patterns is one of the best investments you can make. First, they give you a shared vocabulary with other developers. When someone in a code review says 'this looks like a God Class, can you split it using the Single Responsibility Principle,' you immediately know what they mean instead of being confused. Or when your tech lead says 'we should use Strategy pattern for the discount rules,' you understand the proposal without a long explanation. Second, patterns help you recognise solutions in code you read. When you join a company and see at-Transactional everywhere, knowing it's the Proxy pattern helps you understand what Spring is doing behind the scenes. You're not just using magic annotations — you understand the design. Third, patterns are absolutely essential for interviews. Almost every Java interview will ask about Singleton, Factory, or patterns in Spring Boot. Not knowing them is a red flag. Fourth, patterns prevent you from reinventing the wheel. The problems they solve — flexible object creation, adding behavior without modifying classes, decoupling components — come up constantly in production code. Having proven solutions ready saves you time and prevents bugs. Fifth, patterns help you learn frameworks faster. When you realise Spring uses Singleton for bean scope and Proxy for AOP, you understand Spring's architecture, not just its syntax. The mistake freshers make is thinking patterns are just interview trivia. They're not. They're the language of software design. When you can discuss patterns fluently, you communicate better, design better, and grow faster as a developer.

speakable_v2.hook: Design patterns pay off for freshers in three ways — and vocabulary is the one most people underestimate.

content.label: Vocabulary
content.text: When a senior says 'use a Strategy here', you need to know what that means to follow the conversation. Without pattern vocabulary, you're locked out of design discussions.

content.label: Proven solutions
content.text: You don't have to invent your own way to handle variable object creation. Factory was figured out decades ago with documented trade-offs. You inherit that experience.

content.label: Reading code faster
content.text: Most Spring Boot codebases use patterns without naming them. Recognising them means you spend less time confused and more time contributing.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: The danger for freshers is over-applying patterns. Learn them to communicate and recognise good solutions — not to use as many as possible in every class you write.

questions.question: What is the difference between structural and behavioral design patterns with examples?
questions.title: Structural vs behavioral patterns
questions.direct_answer: Structural patterns organise how classes and objects are composed (e.g., Decorator, Adapter, Facade); behavioral patterns define how objects communicate and assign responsibilities (e.g., Observer, Strategy, Command).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can correctly categorise patterns and give concrete examples
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up structural and behavioral — e.g., calling Observer structural
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real Spring Boot example of each to demonstrate practical knowledge

sections.title: Structure vs Communication
sections.content:
**Structural patterns** solve problems about how you **compose** classes and objects into larger structures. They focus on **relationships between entities** — how they're assembled, adapted, or organised. Think of them like architectural blueprints showing how rooms connect in a building. Examples: **Adapter** converts one interface to another so incompatible classes can work together; **Decorator** wraps objects to add responsibilities without modifying the original; **Facade** provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem; **Proxy** controls access to another object. **Behavioral patterns** solve problems about how objects **communicate** and **distribute responsibilities**. They focus on **interaction and algorithms** — how objects talk to each other and who does what. Think of them like protocols defining how people interact. Examples: **Observer** defines a one-to-many dependency so when one object changes, all dependents are notified; **Strategy** encapsulates algorithms to make them interchangeable; **Command** encapsulates requests as objects.

The key distinction: structural is about **composition and organisation**, behavioral is about **communication and responsibility**.

sections.title: Structural vs Behavioral at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Structural|~Composition|how objects assemble|Adapter, Decorator|Facade, Proxy
blue|Behavioral|~Communication|how objects interact|Observer, Strategy|Command, Template
emerald|Spring split|~Concrete examples|Proxy = structural|Events = behavioral|@Transactional vs @EventListener
violet|Common trap|~Observer is behavioral|not structural|it's about events|frequent mix-up

sections.title: Structural vs Behavioral in Code
Structural vs Behavioral Patterns
sections.content:
| Aspect | Structural Patterns | Behavioral Patterns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | How objects are composed | How objects communicate |
| Main concern | Class/object structure and relationships | Algorithms and responsibility distribution |
| GoF examples | Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy | Observer, Strategy, Command, Template |
| Spring example | Proxy for @Transactional | Observer for ApplicationEvent listeners |
| Question they answer | How do we assemble components? | How do objects interact and divide work? |

sections.title: When to Apply Each Category
sections.content:
Use **structural patterns** when you need to **organise or adapt existing classes**.

Use **Adapter** when integrating a third-party payment gateway with a different interface than your code expects — you create an adapter class that translates between interfaces.

Use **Decorator** to add logging or caching around a service without modifying the service class.

Use **Facade** to simplify a complex order processing system (payment, inventory, shipping) behind a single OrderService.checkout() method.

Use **behavioral patterns** when you need **flexible algorithms or communication**.

Use **Strategy** when discount calculation rules change (percentage, fixed amount, buy-one-get-one) — you define a DiscountStrategy interface and swap implementations at runtime.

Use **Observer** when multiple systems need to react to events — when an order is placed, email, inventory, and analytics all get notified independently.

Use **Command** to implement undo functionality or queue operations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Observer structural**: Freshers think Observer is structural because it 'connects' objects, but it's behavioral because it defines runtime communication protocols, not compile-time composition.
- **Confusing Decorator and Strategy**: Both seem to 'wrap' behavior, but Decorator adds responsibilities to an object (structural composition), while Strategy swaps algorithms (behavioral interaction).
- **Not giving Spring examples**: Discussing patterns abstractly without mentioning that Spring uses Proxy (structural) for at-Transactional and Observer (behavioral) for ApplicationEvent listeners — interviewers want to see you connect theory to practice.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Structural = composition**: How classes and objects are assembled — Adapter, Decorator, Facade, Proxy, Composite, Bridge, Flyweight
- **Behavioral = communication**: How objects interact and assign responsibilities — Observer, Strategy, Command, Template Method, Iterator, State
- **Structural solves 'what'**: What structure should our classes have to achieve flexibility in composition?
- **Behavioral solves 'how'**: How should objects communicate and who's responsible for which behavior?
- **Spring Proxy is structural**: @Transactional wraps your class in a proxy (composition) to add transaction management without modifying your code
- **Spring Events are behavioral**: ApplicationEvent and @EventListener implement Observer pattern for decoupled communication between components
- **Different dimensions**: Structural addresses static relationships at compile time; behavioral addresses dynamic interactions at runtime

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Structural patterns and behavioral patterns solve different kinds of problems. Structural patterns are about composition — how you organise and assemble classes and objects into larger structures. They focus on relationships. For example, the Decorator pattern wraps an object to add responsibilities without changing its code. You might wrap a CartService with a LoggingCartService that logs every method call. The Proxy pattern controls access to an object — Spring uses this for at-Transactional, wrapping your service class in a proxy that manages database transactions. Adapter converts one interface to another so incompatible classes can work together. These are all about structure and composition. Behavioral patterns are about communication and responsibility. They define how objects interact and who does what. The Observer pattern creates a one-to-many relationship where one object notifies multiple dependents. Spring Events use this — when you publish an OrderPlacedEvent, multiple at-EventListener methods can react independently. Strategy pattern encapsulates algorithms to make them interchangeable at runtime. You might have a DiscountStrategy interface with different implementations for percentage discounts, fixed discounts, or seasonal promotions. Command pattern encapsulates requests as objects, useful for undo operations or job queues. The key difference: structural is about how things are built and connected, behavioral is about how they talk and cooperate. Structural happens at compile time when you define class relationships; behavioral happens at runtime when objects actually communicate. The mistake freshers make is calling Observer a structural pattern because it 'connects' objects. It's behavioral because it defines a communication protocol, not a composition structure. In Spring Boot, Proxy is structural because it's about wrapping and composition, while Events are behavioral because they're about runtime communication between decoupled components.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Structural versus behavioral is the GoF distinction interviewers use most — and callers often mix them up.

beats.content: Structural patterns are about composition — how you assemble classes and objects into larger structures. Ask: how are things put together? Decorator wraps objects to add behaviour. Adapter translates one interface into another. Facade simplifies a complex subsystem.

Behavioral patterns are about communication and responsibility — how objects interact and who does what. Ask: how do things talk and share work? Observer notifies subscribers of state changes. Strategy swaps algorithms at runtime. Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton with steps that subclasses fill in.

In Spring: AOP proxies are structural — they wrap beans to add cross-cutting behaviour. Template Method is behavioral — JdbcTemplate defines the connection and error-handling skeleton, you supply the SQL.

speakable_v2.cap: gotcha: Observer is behavioral, not structural — it's about event communication, not object assembly. This is a frequent mix-up in interviews.

questions.question: Which design patterns are most commonly used in Java Spring Boot development?
questions.title: Design patterns used in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot internally uses many patterns: Singleton (all Spring beans are singletons by default), Factory (ApplicationContext creates beans), Proxy (AOP, @Transactional), Template Method (JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate), Observer (Spring Events), and Decorator (security filter chains). Knowing these helps you understand Spring internals.

interviewer_intent.testing: Connecting abstract patterns to the framework you will use every day
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Discussing patterns only in abstract — interviewers want to see Spring connection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name 4-5 patterns with specific Spring examples for each

sections.title: Design Patterns Built Into Spring Boot
sections.content:
Spring Framework is essentially a collection of design patterns implemented for you. When you write a Spring Boot app, you're using patterns even if you don't realise it. **Singleton** is the default scope for all Spring beans — one shared instance per application context. **Factory** is how the **ApplicationContext** creates and manages beans based on configuration and annotations. **Proxy** wraps your beans to add cross-cutting concerns: when you annotate a method with **@Transactional**, Spring creates a proxy around your class that starts and commits database transactions. **Template Method** is in **JdbcTemplate** and **RestTemplate** — they define the skeleton of an algorithm (connect to DB, execute query, close connection) and let you customise specific steps. **Observer** pattern powers **Spring Events** — you publish an event and multiple listeners react independently. **Dependency Injection** itself is an application of the **Dependency Inversion Principle** using Factory and Strategy patterns.

Understanding these patterns helps you debug Spring behaviour and design your own components following Spring's conventions.

sections.title: Spring's Built-in Patterns
sections.content:
amber|Singleton|~Default bean scope|one shared instance|@Service / @Component|reused everywhere
blue|Factory|~ApplicationContext|creates + wires beans|by annotation/config|getBean()
emerald|Proxy|~AOP wrappers|@Transactional|@Cacheable, @Async|self-calls bypass it
violet|Template / Observer|~Boilerplate + events|JdbcTemplate|RestTemplate|ApplicationEvent listeners

sections.title: Spring Patterns in a Cart Service
When You're Already Using These Patterns
sections.content: You're using **Singleton** every time you inject a service with **@Autowired** or constructor injection — Spring ensures only one instance exists. You're using **Factory** when Spring's **ApplicationContext** instantiates your beans based on **@Component**, **@Service**, **@Repository** annotations. You're using **Proxy** whenever you use **@Transactional**, **@Cacheable**, or **@Async** — Spring wraps your method in additional logic without you writing that code. You're using **Template Method** when calling **JdbcTemplate.query()** or **RestTemplate.getForObject()** — the template handles connection management, you just provide the query or URL. You're using **Observer** with **@EventListener** for decoupled communication — when an order is placed, multiple systems (email, inventory, analytics) can react without the order service knowing about them.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not recognising patterns in action**: Freshers use **@Transactional** daily but don't realise it's the Proxy pattern — interviewers expect you to make this connection.
- **Thinking Spring is the pattern**: Saying 'Spring is a Singleton pattern' instead of 'Spring uses Singleton pattern for bean scope' shows confusion between framework and pattern.
- **Ignoring why patterns matter**: Just listing patterns without explaining how they help (Singleton reduces memory, Proxy adds behavior without code changes) misses the practical value interviewers want to hear.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Singleton everywhere**: All Spring beans are singletons by default unless you specify a different scope like prototype or request
- **ApplicationContext is a Factory**: Spring's container creates and manages beans based on annotations and configuration files
- **Proxy for AOP**: Annotations like @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async work by wrapping your class in a proxy that adds behavior at runtime
- **Template Method in Spring templates**: JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, JmsTemplate all use Template Method pattern to handle boilerplate code
- **Observer via Events**: Spring's event publishing mechanism (ApplicationEventPublisher and @EventListener) implements Observer pattern
- **Dependency Injection uses Factory and Strategy**: Spring injects dependencies and swaps implementations based on configuration without code changes
- **Interview gold**: Connecting patterns to Spring features you've used shows practical understanding, not just theory

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot is built on design patterns, so you're using them even if you don't realise it. The most common is Singleton — every Spring bean is a singleton by default, meaning Spring creates one instance and reuses it across the application. That's why you can inject the same service into multiple controllers and they all share the same instance. Factory pattern is how Spring's ApplicationContext works. When you annotate a class with at-Service or at-Component, the ApplicationContext acts as a factory that creates and manages those beans for you. Proxy is huge in Spring. When you put at-Transactional on a method, Spring doesn't modify your code — it wraps your class in a proxy that starts a transaction before the method and commits it after. Same with at-Cacheable and at-Async. Template Method is in JdbcTemplate and RestTemplate. These classes handle all the boilerplate like opening connections, error handling, and cleanup, while you just provide the specific query or endpoint. Observer pattern powers Spring Events. You publish an event with ApplicationEventPublisher, and multiple at-EventListener methods can react to it independently, which keeps your code decoupled. The mistake freshers make is talking about patterns abstractly. In an interview, always connect patterns to Spring features you've actually used. Say 'at-Transactional uses Proxy pattern' instead of just listing pattern names. That shows you understand how patterns solve real problems in the framework you'll work with every day.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Spring Boot is basically a showcase of design patterns — and naming which ones it uses is the answer interviewers love to hear.

content: Singleton — every @Component and @Service bean is a singleton by default
Factory — ApplicationContext creates and wires all your beans
Proxy — @Transactional wraps your class in a CGLIB proxy to manage transaction boundaries
Template Method — JdbcTemplate handles connection boilerplate, you supply only the SQL
Observer — ApplicationEventPublisher lets beans publish and subscribe to events

beats.content: Knowing these patterns explains why Spring behaves the way it does. When a self-invoked method skips @Transactional, it's because the proxy can't intercept internal calls — the Proxy pattern has a specific limitation there.

speakable_v2.cap: production trap: Self-invoked methods bypass Spring's proxy, so @Transactional and @Cacheable won't fire. Knowing the Proxy pattern is what makes that behaviour make sense.

questions.question: What is the difference between a design pattern and an algorithm?
questions.title: Design pattern vs algorithm — concept vs computation
questions.direct_answer: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure to solve a specific computational problem (like sorting or searching) — it is deterministic and directly implementable. A design pattern is a general template for structuring code to solve a design problem — it is abstract and must be adapted to context. Algorithms solve computation; patterns solve structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can clearly distinguish the two concepts
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as similar — algorithms are computational, patterns are structural
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one example of each category to make the distinction concrete

sections.title: Algorithms Compute, Patterns Structure
sections.content:
An **algorithm** is a precise sequence of steps to solve a computational problem — it's like a recipe with exact instructions. **Binary search** is an algorithm: split the sorted array in half, compare the target with the middle element, repeat on one half until found. It's **deterministic** (same input always produces same output) and **directly implementable** (you write the code exactly as the algorithm describes). A **design pattern** is a high-level template for solving a recurring design problem — it's like a blueprint, not a finished building. The **Strategy pattern** says 'define a family of algorithms and make them interchangeable,' but it doesn't tell you what those algorithms do or how to code them. You must **adapt** the pattern to your context: discount strategies, payment strategies, sorting strategies. Patterns are about **structure and relationships** between classes; algorithms are about **computation and logic**.

In Java terms, an algorithm is the method body; a pattern is the class design.

sections.title: Algorithm vs Pattern at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Algorithm|~Computation|deterministic steps|binary search, mergesort|same code every time
blue|Pattern|~Structure|abstract template|Strategy, Factory|adapt to context
emerald|In code|~Where they live|algorithm = method body|pattern = class design|different levels
violet|Both reusable|~Different reuse|algorithm: same problem|pattern: many domains|don't confuse them

sections.title: Algorithm vs Pattern in Code
Algorithm vs Design Pattern
sections.content:
| Aspect | Algorithm | Design Pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Solves computational problem | Solves structural design problem |
| Specificity | Concrete step-by-step procedure | Abstract template needing adaptation |
| Implementation | Code matches algorithm exactly | Code varies based on context |
| Example | Merge sort, Dijkstra's algorithm | Singleton, Factory, Observer |
| Reusability | Reuse for same problem type | Reuse across different domains |

sections.title: When Each Concept Applies
sections.content:
Use **algorithms** when you have a clear computational task: sorting a list (use quicksort or mergesort), finding the shortest path in a graph (use Dijkstra's), or searching in a data structure (use binary search for sorted arrays, hash lookup for maps). The algorithm tells you exactly what to do.

Use **design patterns** when you have a structural problem: you need objects created in a controlled way (use Factory or Singleton), you want to add behavior without modifying classes (use Decorator or Proxy), or you need objects to communicate flexibly (use Observer or Strategy). The pattern gives you a structure to implement in your own way. In a Spring Boot cart service, you'd use **binary search algorithm** to find a product in a sorted list, but you'd use **Strategy pattern** to structure how different discount rules are applied.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling Strategy an algorithm**: Freshers say 'Strategy pattern is an algorithm for swapping behaviors' — it's a pattern for structuring interchangeable algorithms, not an algorithm itself.
- **Thinking algorithms are patterns**: Saying 'I used the binary search pattern' when you mean 'I implemented the binary search algorithm' — patterns structure classes, algorithms compute results.
- **Missing the abstraction level**: Algorithms are concrete and procedural; patterns are abstract and organisational. Confusing the two shows you don't understand that code has both computational logic (algorithms) and structural design (patterns).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Algorithm = computation**: A deterministic, step-by-step procedure to solve a specific computational problem like sorting or searching
- **Pattern = structure**: An abstract template for organizing classes and objects to solve a recurring design problem
- **Algorithms are concrete**: You implement them exactly as defined — mergesort code looks the same regardless of context
- **Patterns are abstract**: You adapt them to context — Factory pattern looks different in payment processing vs object pooling
- **Algorithms in methods**: You write algorithm logic inside methods (the 'how' of computation)
- **Patterns in classes**: You structure classes and their relationships using patterns (the 'what' of design)
- **Both are reusable**: Algorithms solve the same problem repeatedly; patterns solve different problems with similar structure

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure to solve a computational problem. Think of sorting algorithms like quicksort or searching algorithms like binary search. They're deterministic — same input always gives same output — and you implement them exactly as described. If you're coding binary search, you split the array in half, compare the middle element, and repeat. That's the algorithm, and everyone's implementation will look similar. A design pattern is different. It's a high-level template for structuring your code to solve a design problem, not a computation problem. Take the Strategy pattern. It doesn't tell you what algorithms to use; it tells you how to structure your code so you can swap algorithms at runtime. You might use Strategy to switch between different discount calculation methods in a cart service. The pattern gives you the structure — an interface, concrete implementations, and a context class — but you fill in the actual logic yourself. The key difference: algorithms are about computation and logic, patterns are about structure and relationships between classes. In code terms, an algorithm lives in a method body telling you what steps to perform. A pattern lives in your class design telling you how to organize those classes. In an interview, give concrete examples. Say 'mergesort is an algorithm because it's a specific sorting procedure, but Factory is a pattern because it's a template for how to create objects, not what those objects do.' That makes the distinction crystal clear.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Algorithms and design patterns both solve problems — but they solve completely different kinds of problems.

beats.content: QuickSort has one correct implementation — you follow the steps and get a sorted list. The Strategy pattern is different every time you use it. The structure is the same, but what goes inside the strategy classes is completely up to you and your domain.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: Don't say algorithms and patterns are similar. Algorithms compute results; patterns organize code structure. The distinction is the whole answer.

questions.question: What are anti-patterns and can you give examples?
questions.title: Anti-patterns — what they are and common examples
questions.direct_answer: An anti-pattern is a commonly used solution that seems reasonable but actually makes things worse. Unlike design patterns (which are good solutions), anti-patterns are patterns of failure. Common examples: God Class (one class does everything), Spaghetti Code (tangled unstructured code), Golden Hammer (using one pattern for everything), and Copy-Paste Programming (duplicating code instead of abstracting).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the term anti-pattern and can name a few
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the term anti-pattern — it is common vocabulary in design discussions
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name 3-4 antipatterns with a one-line description of each

sections.title: Anti-Patterns Are Patterns of Failure
sections.content:
An **anti-pattern** is a solution that seems like a good idea at first but creates more problems than it solves. While **design patterns** are proven best practices, **anti-patterns** are proven worst practices — common mistakes that keep appearing because they're initially appealing.

Think of them as **patterns of failure**. For example, putting all your code in one giant class (the **God Class** anti-pattern) seems efficient at first — everything's in one place! But it becomes unmaintainable, untestable, and violates single responsibility. Other classic anti-patterns: **Spaghetti Code** (tangled, unstructured logic with no clear flow), **Golden Hammer** (using one solution for every problem — 'I just learned Singleton, so everything's a Singleton now'), **Copy-Paste Programming** (duplicating code instead of abstracting it into reusable methods), and **Magic Numbers** (hardcoding values like 86400 instead of SECONDS_PER_DAY). Recognising anti-patterns is as important as knowing design patterns — it helps you spot bad code in reviews and avoid creating it yourself.

sections.title: Anti-Patterns at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Anti-pattern|~Pattern of failure|looks reasonable|makes things worse|opposite of good design
blue|God Class|~Does everything|breaks SRP|untestable|split by responsibility
emerald|Golden Hammer|~One tool for all|Singleton everywhere|wrong-fit pattern|know the limits
violet|Copy-paste / Magic numbers|~Hidden debt|duplicate logic (DRY)|86400 vs SECONDS_PER_DAY|name your constants

sections.title: Anti-Pattern Examples
When Anti-Patterns Appear
sections.content: Anti-patterns typically emerge under **time pressure** or **lack of experience**. A fresher building their first Spring Boot app might create a **God Class** because they haven't learned separation of concerns yet — one controller handles HTTP, business logic, database access, and email sending. **Golden Hammer** appears when someone learns one pattern and applies it everywhere: 'I'll use Singleton for my database connection, my email service, my logger, my config...' even when Singleton isn't appropriate. **Copy-Paste Programming** happens when you're rushing to meet a deadline and duplicate code instead of refactoring it into a reusable method. The key is recognising these patterns during **code reviews** or **refactoring sessions** and replacing them with proper design patterns. For example, replace God Class with **Single Responsibility Principle** (separate concerns into service, repository, controller), replace Copy-Paste with **Strategy pattern** for algorithm variations.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing the term anti-pattern**: In design discussions and code reviews, terms like God Class and Spaghetti Code are common vocabulary — not knowing them makes you seem inexperienced.
- **Defending anti-patterns**: Freshers sometimes say 'but my God Class works' without understanding that 'works now' doesn't mean 'maintainable later' — anti-patterns create technical debt.
- **Overusing patterns (Golden Hammer)**: Ironically, trying to avoid anti-patterns by using design patterns everywhere creates a different anti-pattern — know when simple code is better than a pattern.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Anti-patterns are bad solutions**: They seem reasonable initially but create maintenance nightmares, unlike design patterns which are proven good solutions
- **God Class**: One class with too many responsibilities — violates Single Responsibility Principle and becomes unmaintainable
- **Spaghetti Code**: Tangled, unstructured code with complex control flow and no clear separation of concerns
- **Golden Hammer**: Using one solution for every problem — 'when you have a hammer, everything looks like a nail'
- **Copy-Paste Programming**: Duplicating code instead of abstracting into reusable methods or classes — violates DRY principle
- **Magic Numbers**: Hardcoding values without named constants — makes code unclear and hard to change
- **Common in code reviews**: Senior developers use anti-pattern names to point out problems — knowing these terms is professional vocabulary

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Anti-patterns are commonly used solutions that seem reasonable at first but actually make things worse. They're the opposite of design patterns — patterns of failure instead of success. The most famous is the God Class, where one class does everything. Imagine a CartService that handles HTTP requests, business logic, database access, payment processing, and email notifications all in one class. It seems efficient because everything's together, but it becomes impossible to test, maintain, or understand. You can't change the email logic without risking the payment code. Spaghetti Code is another classic — tangled, unstructured logic with goto-style jumps and complex nested conditions that no one can follow. Golden Hammer is when you learn one pattern or tool and use it for everything. A fresher learns Singleton and suddenly makes every class a singleton, even when it doesn't need to be. Copy-Paste Programming is duplicating code instead of abstracting it. You copy a discount calculation method three times with slight variations instead of using a Strategy pattern. Magic Numbers are hardcoded values like 86400 in your code when you should use a constant like SECONDS_PER_DAY. The mistake freshers make is not knowing these terms. In code reviews, when a senior developer says 'this is a God Class,' you need to understand what that means and how to fix it. In an interview, naming a few anti-patterns shows you understand not just what to do, but also what not to do, which is equally important in real codebases.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app applying design patterns to a cart service
speakable_v2.hook: Anti-patterns are just as important to know as patterns — they're the solutions that look right but quietly wreck your codebase.

content: God Class — one class does everything, violates Single Responsibility, impossible to test
Spaghetti Code — tangled, unstructured code with no clear separation of concerns
Golden Hammer — using your favourite pattern for every problem regardless of fit
Copy-Paste Programming — duplicating logic instead of extracting shared abstractions

beats.content: The tricky thing about anti-patterns is they often feel like the fast path. Dumping logic into one class feels quick. Copying code avoids the work of abstraction. The cost shows up weeks later when you need to change something.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: God Class is the most common anti-pattern in Spring Boot apps — the service layer grows until one CartService handles cart, checkout, inventory, and notifications all at once.
